newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis return to bombed market, bury their dead.
newsitem.headline: Israelis return to bombed market, bury their dead.

text.p: Putting food on the table for the Jewish Sabbath outweighed security concerns for Israelis who returned on Thursday to a Jerusalem street market where Arab suicide bombers killed 13 people a day earlier.
As life went on in the Mahane Yehuda market, mourners streamed to cemeteries for the funerals of victims of the deadliest attack on Israelis in more than a year.
"The whole family is coming tomorrow and I have to make a big dinner. I have to shop at the market," said Pnina Ashkenazi as she shopped in preparation for her sabbath eve meal.
"I usually do my shopping on Wednesdays. Yesterday, I had to take care of my grandson and that was my luck," she said.
City workers spent the night removing debris and cleaning a covered passage in the market which the two bombers, positioned at both ends, turned into a corridor of death.
Memorial candles flickered on a makeshift shrine at the spot where one of the bombs went off.
Walls were plastered with black-bordered funeral notices. "We mourn the death of Sami Malka who died in a murderous and criminal attack," read one.
At a cemetery overlooking the Judean hills, Malka's wife Ariella spoke to her husband at his graveside.

"Sami, listen. Don't worry about Bar," she said in a calm voice, referring to their three-year-old son. "I will take care of him...but I ask you to watch over us, the whole family and nation, from above."
Then reality hit and she snapped, breaking down in tears as she muttered, "What a shame I am saying goodbye to you. What a pity."
In the market, a vendor stood inside his shop peering out through an open space where his storefront window used to be.
At one end of the passage, shoe boxes spilled out of a stall into the alley. Workers sorted through them to find matching pairs.
Two shopkeepers argued over the wisdom of employing Arab workers.
"I don't care if I have to pay an additional 1,000 shekels ($285) a month, I'll employ Russian Jews," said one.
"You don't know what you are talking about. My Arab employees can come back today, as far as I'm concerned," his colleague replied.
Israel clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the blasts, preventing thousands of Palestinians from going to work in the Jewish state.
The front pages of Israeli newspapers reflected the depth of sorrow and fury over the suicide bombings, publishing huge photos of bloodied and blackened men, women and children wounded by the blasts.
"The terrorism is back," read one front-page headline.

Chemi Shalev, diplomatic correspondent of the Maariv daily, wrote the attack would divert the attention of the United States -- the main Middle East peace broker -- from Israeli settlement construction in Arab East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza.
The settlement issue had already brought peace talks with the Palestinians to a standstill.
Among Jewish shoppers in the market, the mood was a mixture of resignation and defiance.
"What can I do? I have to shop for the sabbath," said Meir Cohen as he picked out tomatoes in the huge market in which longtime Jewish residents of Jerusalem say the heart of the city beats.
Miriam Goldberg said Arab bombs would not drive her away.
"These barbarians, animals of prey, want to throw us out of the country. We won't go," she said as soldiers and police patrolled nearby.
But she lamented: "How much longer? How much longer?"
